description: Original slide figures imported at the author's request.

figures.name: detection-and-segmentation
figures.title: Different outputs from visual perception
figures.caption: Left: object detections are shown as labeled boxes. Right: the lecture contrasts a photographed scene with region-level semantic labels. Compare what information each output preserves. Source: Part I, slide 26 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Original image panels arranged side by side; aspect ratios retained, no redrawing.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Slide credits: Ren, He, Girshick, and Sun, 2015; Fabaret et al., 2012 (spelling retained from the slide).

figures.name: visual-pathway
figures.title: From the eyes to visual cortex
figures.caption: Follow the colored pathways from the two visual fields through the optic nerves and optic chiasm toward the lateral geniculate nucleus and primary visual cortex. Source: Part I, slide 16 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content. Transparency flattened onto the original slide's white background.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Slide lists https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_system and Principles of Neural Science. The deck does not identify this individual illustration more precisely.

figures.name: orientation-selectivity
figures.title: Orientation-selective visual responses
figures.caption: The lecture figure combines a light-bar stimulus, recorded spike trains, and a tuning curve. The visual response varies with bar orientation, illustrating feature selectivity. Source: Part I, slide 17 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Slide credits Hubel and Wiesel, 1959 and links https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3425/12/4/470; this is the supplied schematic, not a newly generated recording.

figures.name: light-surface-camera
figures.title: Illumination, surface reflection, and camera geometry
figures.caption: Trace the path from the light source to the surface, through the optics, and onto the sensor plane. The diagram connects scene illumination to the image-formation discussion. Source: Part II, slide 3 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide/image.

figures.name: electromagnetic-spectrum
figures.title: Visible light within the electromagnetic spectrum
figures.caption: The expanded color band shows the visible region within a much wider range of wavelengths. Read the wavelength labels as the approximate convention used in the lecture. Source: Part I, slide 33 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide/image.

figures.name: pinhole-image-inversion
figures.title: Why the pinhole image is inverted
figures.caption: The original lecture diagram retains the object, the inverted image, and the crossing rays. Trace a ray from the top of the tree to the lower part of the image. Source: Part I, slide 41 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Original slide diagram rendered and cropped; all diagram labels, arrows, and panels retained. Slide title/footer and surrounding prose omitted.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide.

figures.name: pinhole-aperture-comparison
figures.title: Aperture size and image sharpness
figures.caption: The six source images compare the labeled apertures from 2 mm to 0.07 mm. The lecture highlights 0.35 mm in this example and marks diffraction at the smallest openings; this is not a universal optimum. Source: Part I, slide 49 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Original slide diagram rendered and cropped; all diagram labels, arrows, and panels retained. Slide title/footer and surrounding prose omitted.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide.

figures.name: ccd-cmos-readout
figures.title: CCD and CMOS image-sensor readout
figures.caption: The source illustration contrasts charge transfer in a CCD with charge-to-voltage conversion and active-pixel structure in CMOS. Keep the readout architecture separate from the later color-filter pattern. Source: Part I, slide 58 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Embedded Figure 2.24 includes credit text for Litwiller 2001, Photonics Spectra, and an active-pixel illustration URL. Those embedded credits are retained.

figures.name: bayer-filter-system
figures.title: Bayer color sampling
figures.caption: The original diagram connects incoming light, the filter layer, the sensor array, and the resulting Bayer sequence. The colored photosites are samples used to form a color image, not complete RGB triplets. Source: Part I, slide 64 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: OPT logo and source branding embedded in the slide image are retained.

figures.name: cone-spectral-responses
figures.title: Overlapping cone sensitivities
figures.caption: The long-, medium-, and short-wavelength response curves overlap. Use the plotted wavelength axis rather than interpreting the color names as three disjoint spectral bands. Source: Part II, slide 9 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide/image.

figures.name: tristimulus-light-path
figures.title: From a reflected spectrum to three responses
figures.caption: The source figure places the illuminant, surface, and observer beside spectral plots and the three cone-response areas. It provides the visual counterpart to the response integrals above. Source: Part II, slide 12 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Embedded caption: Fig. 10.9, The tristimulus response of the human eye. The lecture reference list includes Peter Corke; no exact edition is assigned to this image.

figures.name: color-matching-functions
figures.title: Color-matching functions
figures.caption: The original plot shows the three wavelength-dependent matching coefficients, including a negative portion of the red coefficient. This leads to the experimental interpretation in the next subsection. Source: Part II, slide 20 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Embedded caption Fig. 10.10 retained as supplied; it contains the historical terminology used by the source figure.

figures.name: color-matching-experiment
figures.title: The color-matching experiment
figures.caption: An observer compares the test-light field with the primary-light mixture. Relate the two fields in this diagram to moving a primary-light contribution from one side of the matching equation to the other. Source: Part II, slide 22 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Slide credits Monaci, Menegaz, Susstrunk, and Knoblauch (2002), Color contrast detection in spatial chromatic noise; the bibliographic wording is not independently expanded.

figures.name: rgb-pixels-and-values
figures.title: A color image is an array of numbers
figures.caption: The enlarged sample region connects a familiar color image with channel values stored at individual pixel locations. The numerical array and the displayed image are two representations of the same input. Source: Part II, slide 36 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide/image.

figures.name: rgb-channel-decomposition
figures.title: The image and its separate RGB channels
figures.caption: The full-color source image appears beside the lecture's red-, green-, and blue-channel views. Inspect how the same facial features contribute differently to the three channels. Source: Part I, slide 66 [[1]](#vision-ref-1).
figures.transform: Original color image and original three-channel panel combined with white spacing; no recoloring.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: No separate original-source attribution was established from the selected slide/image.

figures.name: color-space-image-channels
figures.title: Alternative channel representations
figures.caption: The source figure shows a color scene and several channel views, including the hue, saturation, and value views identified in its original caption. Compare the structures retained by each representation. Source: Part II, slide 30 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.
figures.credit_on_slide_or_image: Embedded caption Fig. 10.15 retained. The supplied slide connects this figure with color-space conversion.

figures.name: pixel-brightness-operations
figures.title: Point-wise changes in appearance
figures.caption: The embedded source image compares the original with darkening, lightening, and inversion. The lecture displays the darkening and lightening panels; the full extracted illustration also retains its labeled inversion panel. Source: Part II, slide 42 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
figures.transform: Embedded image exported without changing its content.

figures.name: threshold-and-intensity-transforms
figures.title: Thresholding and intensity transformations
figures.caption: The upper-right panel shows the binary thresholded image. Compare it with the original at upper left; the other panels and their transfer curves show additional intensity transformations included in the source illustration. Source: Part II, slide 43 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).

figures.caption: The highlighted input window contributes to the highlighted output location. This is the original lecture illustration of the mask, kernel, or filter operation. Source: Part II, slide 44 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).

figures.title: The visual effect of averaging
figures.caption: The original and smoothed portraits illustrate the loss of fine detail. The lecture identifies the example as smoothing with a 21 by 21 averaging kernel. Source: Part II, slide 50 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).

figures.caption: The source image shows the one-dimensional profile, the two-dimensional weighting surface, and an intensity view of the kernel. These are complementary views of the weighting discussed in this section. Source: Part II, slide 51 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).

figures.title: Increasing the Gaussian scale
figures.caption: The lecture pairs broader weighting curves with progressively smoother images, labeled with sigma values of 4, 8, 16, and 32. Observe the loss of edge detail rather than treating smoothing as uniformly beneficial. Source: Part II, slide 57 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).

figures.title: Combining two corresponding pixels
figures.caption: Two input images contribute to one output image. The highlighted rows and columns identify the corresponding pixel locations used in the dyadic operation. Source: Part II, slide 58 [[2]](#vision-ref-2).
